metaDescription: Six 6 gallon RV water heaters compared on gas, electric and hybrid fuel, aluminum versus porcelain tanks, ignition type and cutout fit.
expertTake: The Suburban SAW6DEL is the pick for most replacements because it fits the existing cutout and uses direct spark ignition. The Elk Mountain is the pick if you want a maintenance-free aluminum tank with gas and electric. Skip a gas heater for a rig that never sees propane, where a plug-in electric tank is simpler.
introParagraphs: The classic RV water heater is a small tank in a cabinet with a door on the outside wall. It runs on propane, often with an optional electric element, and its job is simple: have hot water ready when you turn the tap.

Choosing a replacement is mostly about three things. The fuel and ignition type decide whether it works in your rig, the tank material decides how much maintenance it needs, and the cutout size decides whether it fits without carpentry. This guide compares the lineup on those points.

products.name: Suburban SAW6DEL 6 Gallon Direct Fit RV Water Heater DSI
products.description:
Suburban's Advantage Direct Fit heater is built to drop into an existing cutout without modifications to the cabinet or the exterior wall. That is the biggest hidden cost in a water heater swap, because moving a cutout means carpentry and sealing. It uses direct spark ignition, so there is no standing pilot to relight or shut off before fueling.

The tank is porcelain-lined steel, a residential-style design that holds heat well but needs an anode rod and attention. DSI requires 12 volt power for the spark, so a low battery can cause ignition lockout. It sits in the upper price tier.

Compared with the Elk Mountain, it offers a proven brand and fit but requires anode maintenance. Check the anode yearly and keep batteries charged. In year three the wear items are the anode rod and the igniter, and a clean burner tube and a charged battery prevent most no-light calls. Keep a spare anode in the drawer.
products.bestFor: Replacing a Suburban or similar heater without changing the cutout.
pros: Direct fit with no cutout changes
Direct spark ignition, no standing pilot

products.name: Elk Mountain WH-6GEA 6 Gallon Gas and Electric Heater 12V
products.description:
The Elk Mountain WH-6GEA is a gas and electric heater with an aluminum tank that needs no anode rod, which removes the most forgotten maintenance task in RV life. A steel tank rusts from the inside as the anode is consumed, while an aluminum tank does not rust the same way. The listing gives the dimensions, 16 by 16 by 14 inches, so you can check against your cutout.

Gas plus electric means you can run on propane off-grid or on shore power at a campground, and you can run both to speed recovery. A 12 volt feed powers the ignition. It sits in the lowest price tier among the gas units here.

Compared with the Suburban, it gives up the direct-fit promise and the established brand, but the aluminum tank saves upkeep. Verify the cutout dimensions before ordering. Because the tank is aluminum, flushing for sediment becomes the main chore, along with a clean burner tube. Photograph your old unit's door and vent before removal so the new one matches. Test both fuel modes at the first fill so you know each element works.
products.bestFor: Owners who want gas and electric with no anode maintenance.
pros: Aluminum tank needs no anode rod
Lowest price tier among gas units

products.name: Dometic WH-6GA 6 Gallon Gas-Only RV Water Heater
products.description:
Dometic's WH-6GA is a gas-only heater with electronic ignition and no anode rod to service. It fits rigs that only ever use propane, or boondockers who do not want to rely on shore power. Fewer systems means fewer parts to fail.

The tradeoff is that you cannot heat with a campground hookup, so recovery relies on the gas burner alone. It sits in the upper-middle price tier. Dometic is a major RV component brand, which makes parts and dealers easy to find.

Compared with the Elk Mountain, it drops the electric element and gains a bigger brand name. Confirm that it matches your door and vent cutout. Because it is gas only, confirm your propane supply and regulator are in good shape before ordering. A gas-only heater with a weak regulator is a common cause of slow recovery. Run the burner for a minute after installing and watch for a steady blue flame.
products.bestFor: Propane-only and off-grid rigs that want a major brand.
pros: Major RV brand with easy parts

products.name: Suburban SW6D 6 Gallon RV Water Heater DSI
products.description:
The Suburban SW6D uses a porcelain-lined steel tank with a replaceable anode rod and offers an optional electric element for campsite or generator power. It uses direct spark ignition. This is the classic Suburban design that many RVs have used for years.

The replaceable anode is both the strength and the chore: inspect it yearly and replace it at about 75 percent consumed. Hard water eats it faster. The optional electric element widens the power options. It sits in the middle price tier.

Compared with the Elk Mountain, it demands anode maintenance but follows a familiar service path. Keep the door and burner area clean of spider webs. Because it is a familiar design, parts and service information are easy to find. Check the pressure and temperature relief valve every spring.
products.bestFor: Owners who want the familiar Suburban design with a replaceable anode.
cons: Steel tank can rust if neglected

products.name: CAMPLUX 6 Gallon RV Propane and Electric Hybrid Heater
products.description:
CAMPLUX's hybrid heater runs on propane for off-grid use, electric at RV parks, or both together for faster recovery. It is engineered for standard 13 by 13 inch cutouts with a 15 by 15 inch exterior, which is the common size for 4 to 6 gallon RV tanks. The mode and temperature can be set from inside without stepping outside.

The indoor control is a real convenience in bad weather. The tank is porcelain with an anode rod, so the usual anode maintenance applies. It sits in the upper-middle price tier.

Compared with the Suburban, it adds hybrid modes and indoor control but is a newer brand. Check the door and vent fit before ordering. Test the indoor controls when you install and confirm that each mode lights as expected. Keep the batteries charged for ignition. Leave the unit on hybrid mode when you first light it to confirm both sources work.
products.bestFor: Rigs that want propane, electric and hybrid control from inside.

products.name: CAMPLUX 6 Gallon Electric Mini-Tank Heater 1440W
products.description:
This CAMPLUX is a corded 120 volt point-of-use tank with a glass-lined interior, insulation foam and three temperature settings. It carries a UL approval claim. It is not a gas heater, so it does not need a vented cutout or propane line.

That makes it a different tool: a plug-in heater for a van, a cabin or a far bathroom, not a direct replacement for a propane RV heater. At 1440 watts it needs shore power or a generator. It sits in the low price tier.

Compared with the gas units, it is simpler to install but cannot run off-grid. At 1440 watts, plan on about 12 amps at 120 volts and check the pedestal circuit. Drain the tank before freezing weather. Use a ground-fault outlet and keep the cord off the floor.
products.bestFor: Vans and cabins with shore power that do not need propane.
cons: Not a drop-in for a propane heater

buyingCriteria.explanation: Gas-only units like the Dometic work off-grid. The Elk Mountain and CAMPLUX hybrid add electric. The CAMPLUX plug-in is electric only at about 12 amps. Match the fuel to how you camp. A rule of thumb is to take photos of the old unit, the door, the vent and the cutout, because those details decide whether a replacement fits. Always confirm the vent and door match the new unit before cutting any sealant.

Suburban's SAW6DEL and SW6D use direct spark ignition, which lights on demand and needs 12 volt power, with no standing pilot. A battery below about 10.5 volts can lock out ignition. Pilot models keep a flame and must be shut off before fueling. If your heater has a pilot, remember to shut it off before refueling, and consider a DSI model so there is no pilot to forget.

Elk Mountain and Dometic use aluminum tanks that need no anode. Suburban and the hybrid CAMPLUX use porcelain-lined steel with an anode rod to inspect yearly. Aluminum saves chores, while lined steel holds heat well. A weak battery is the most common reason a DSI heater will not light, so check the house battery before blaming the heater.

The CAMPLUX hybrid fits a 13 by 13 inch cutout with a 15 by 15 inch exterior. The Elk Mountain is 16 by 16 by 14 inches. The Suburban Direct Fit needs no cutout changes. Measure first. Treat the relief valve as a safety part, not an accessory, and never cap or plug it.

Running gas and electric together speeds recovery when power is available. A 6 gallon tank supplies about two short showers before the mix cools. Flush the tank every year, because sediment lowers recovery and causes rumbling noises.

A temperature and pressure relief valve is required on tank units, and you must never plug it. Bypass and fully drain the tank in winter, and never leave antifreeze in it. Check the gas supply and regulator, because a heater cannot burn what the line cannot deliver. Keep a simple log of the dates you flushed the tank and checked the anode, because it makes troubleshooting easier.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fit and install
howWeEvaluated.description: We favored direct-fit and standard-cutout designs. Suburban led. We compared direct-fit and standard-cutout designs because carpentry is the hidden cost of a swap.

howWeEvaluated.title: Maintenance load
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared aluminum and lined steel tanks. We counted anode-free tanks as a real maintenance advantage.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fuel flexibility
howWeEvaluated.description: We looked at gas, electric and hybrid options. We read fuel options against how most owners camp.

cards.text: Elk Mountain and Dometic need no anode and avoid the main maintenance chore.

cards.label: Porcelain steel
cards.text: Suburban and the CAMPLUX hybrid hold heat well but need a yearly anode check.

howToChoose.note: Choose aluminum if you will forget the anode.

cards.text: The same cutout size, the same fuel and the same door. Take photos of the old unit before removal.

maintenance.why: A consumed anode lets the steel tank rust. Do it with the heater cold and the water off.
Sediment lowers recovery and causes rumbling. Drain until the water runs clear.
Spider webs cause yellow flame and no ignition. Use a pipe cleaner or small brush.
A stuck valve cannot protect the tank. Lift the lever briefly and look for water.
Bypass and drain the tank, never leave antifreeze in it. Check the drain plug seal as well. Keep a small repair kit with a spare fuse and a few feet of hose.

faq.q: Is a 6 gallon heater big enough?
faq.a: For two people with short showers, yes. Larger families may want 10 gallons or a tankless unit. A larger tank only helps if you need hot water back to back, because most RV showers use the water in short bursts.

faq.q: How much does a 6 gallon heater cost?
faq.a: Prices range from a low tier to an upper tier. Check the listing. Prices change, so compare tiers and what is included, such as a door, an anode and mounting hardware.
Only with a steel tank. Aluminum tanks do not use one. Spring no-hot-water calls are almost always a bypass valve left in the wrong position.

faq.q: Why no hot water in spring?
faq.a: The most common cause is a bypass valve left in the winterize position. A heater that lights and then drops out often needs a cleaned burner tube or a stronger battery.
Direct spark ignition. It lights on demand and needs 12 volt power. Never leave antifreeze in the tank, because it is hard on anode rods and the water supply.

Many last years with annual flushing and anode care. Check your cutout size in inches before ordering, because the door and vent differ by model. Recovery depends on the fuel, the inlet water temperature and whether gas and electric run together.
